newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel tax reforms clear German Bundestag.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel tax reforms clear German Bundestag.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax-cutting reform package cleared Germany's Bundestag lower house of parliament on Thursday, but the legislation faces certain rejection in the opposition-led upper house.
The 1998 and 1999 tax bills, which envisage net tax cuts of 30 billion marks ($17.4 billion), passed by comfortable majorities with the backing of deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition.
Waigel told the chamber the reforms would meet the challenge posed by globalisation by attracting investment and creating new jobs in Germany's unemployment-hit economy.
He also said big income and corporate tax cuts over the next two years would actually revive failing state revenues by boosting economic growth and slashing ways to avoid paying tax.
"I am convinced...that such a structural change in the tax system and a cut in tax rates would not lead to a fall in tax revenues, but a stabilisation and a long-term rise," he said.

The tax reform, which underwent minor amendments in the committee stage, foresees cutting the lowest rate of income tax to 15 percent in 1999 from 39 percent, while the top rate would fall to 39 percent from 53.
The so-called solidarity income tax surcharge -- raised to help regenerate ex-communist eastern Germany -- would fall by two percentage points to 5.5 percent next year.
And the top rate of corporation tax would fall in two steps to 35 percent by 1999 from 45 percent now. A range of tax breaks would be scrapped to offset the tax cuts.

Opposition speakers attacked the financing of the reforms, which they said would leave a budget gap of 45 billion marks. They said to close the gap Waigel would have to announce a hike in value-added tax -- after next year's general election.

"The government's policy will neither revive the economy nor create jobs -- it is the writing on the wall for doing business in Germany and for the welfare state," said Christine Scheel, finance spokeswoman for the opposition Greens party.
Intervening in the debate, opposition Social Democrat (SPD) parliamentary chief Rudolf Scharping said: "This is a deceitful tax reform, and it will not get the support of the SPD."

Without referring to tough borrowing targets for Europe's planned single currency, Waigel did say he was searching for more budget savings to make room for tax cuts. The cabinet is due to sign off on the 1998 budget on July 11.

The tax bills now move on for review by the SPD-controlled Bundesrat upper house of parliament on July 4. The SPD said it would reject the measures, landing them in parliament's drawn-out conflict resolution process.
Kohl, who did not take part in the tax debate, said earlier he still expected to reach agreement with the SPD on tax by the autumn in the mediation committee.
"For 35 years this has been a ritual with all such laws: we'll talk and then in the autumn there will be a tax reform," Kohl told SAT1 television in an interview to be aired later.
"It will not be identical to the tax reform we adopt today -- that belongs to the way parliamentary mediation works. But there will be significant progress. There will be a tax cut."

In stark contrast to the confrontational tax debate, the SPD backed Kohl's coalition to pass Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt's bill to secure state aid to eastern Germany after the current funding plan runs out in 1998.
According to the bill, 5.7 billion marks will be made available per year from 1999 onwards in the form of investment bonuses for companies.
"The east German economy, which is already doing better, will thus gain extra momentum," Rexrodt said. ($ = 1.727 German Marks)
